prompt: What is a career ladder for, by the lesson?
hint: From a feeling to a written answer.

choices.text: Setting salaries
choices.why: Pay bands may follow levels, but the lesson’s purpose is a shared written answer.

choices.text: Turning “is this person senior?” into a question with a written answer that the person, the manager and a panel all read
choices.why: Right: the levels exist anyway; writing them down makes them shared and checkable.

choices.text: Deciding how long each level takes
choices.why: A ladder is not a schedule.

choices.text: Giving managers a list of boxes to tick
choices.why: The lesson warns against treating it as a checklist.

prompt: What goes wrong when levels exist only in managers’ heads? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Salaries go down
choices.why: Not a consequence the lesson names.

choices.text: Nobody gets promoted
choices.why: Promotions still happen, unevenly.

choices.text: The same work earns different titles under different managers
choices.why: Yes: a career depends on who you report to.

choices.text: Nobody can check a decision
choices.why: Yes: a refusal against an unwritten standard cannot be explained or appealed.

choices.text: People cannot tell what to work on
choices.why: Yes: and the confident guess best.

prompt: Match each of Caju’s four dimensions with the question it answers.

pairs.right: how big a piece of work can this person own?
how clear must the problem be before they run with it?
whose work, beyond theirs, gets better because of them?
how good is the work itself?

right_distractors: how many years have they been in the industry?

prompt: A manager tells an engineer, “Going by the ladder, you’ll be senior in eighteen months.” What is wrong with that?
hint: What the ladder does not contain.

choices.text: Eighteen months is too short for anybody to move from mid-level to senior at a company like Caju
choices.why: The objection is to promising a time at all, not to this particular number.

choices.text: A ladder is not a schedule
choices.why: Right: nothing in it says how long a level takes, so the promise has no support.

choices.text: Only the panel may talk about levels
choices.why: Managers talk about levels all the time; this is about the promise.

choices.text: The ladder is revised every year
choices.why: True at Caju, but not the problem with the sentence.

prompt: What separates E3 from E2 on Caju’s ladder?
hint: Not doing the same things better.

choices.text: More years at the company
choices.why: Years are deliberately not on the ladder.

choices.text: Writing more code per week
choices.why: Output volume is not one of the four dimensions.

choices.text: Fewer pull requests coming back
choices.why: That is in the E2 craft row already.

choices.text: Larger scope, a vaguer starting point, and effect beyond their own work
choices.why: Right: an excellent E2 still needs somebody to frame the problem first.

prompt: Put the three tests inside the E3 autonomy row in the order the lesson lists them.
An engineer built a feature flawlessly from a design Diego had already broken into tasks. Which E3 autonomy test does that fail?

choices.text: Other people worked from it
choices.why: That test depends on there being a plan of hers in the first place.

choices.text: The craft row, since flawless code is expected at every level including E1 and E2
choices.why: The craft is fine; the gap is in autonomy.

choices.text: The problem was ambiguous
choices.why: Right: somebody else broke it down, so she executed a plan, however well.

choices.text: None: flawless delivery meets all three
choices.why: Delivery quality is not what the autonomy row measures.

prompt: Why does the lesson say counting years penalises some people unfairly?
hint: Who has fewer years for the same growth?

choices.text: Older engineers are paid too much
choices.why: Pay is not the argument.

choices.text: Years are hard to verify
choices.why: They are easy to verify; that is not the problem.

choices.text: Years reward starting young and never taking a break, and penalise people who had a child, cared for a parent or changed careers
choices.why: Right: years correlate with circumstances a company should not reward for their own sake.

choices.text: Juniors complain
choices.why: Not the reason given.

prompt: A candidate was “senior engineer” at a ten-person startup, where they owned everything. Caju levels them at E2. By the lesson, is that a contradiction?

choices.text: Yes: a senior title should carry over
choices.why: Titles do not carry over; the work is what is levelled.

choices.text: Yes, because owning everything at a startup is more scope than any area at Caju could ever offer
choices.why: Owning everything at ten people is not the same as owning an area, with its operation, at ninety.

choices.text: No, because startups have no real engineering
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim.

choices.text: No: the evidence is read against Caju’s row, not the old title
choices.why: Right: scope and expectations differ between companies, and a past title is not evidence of the row.

prompt: Why is Caju’s M1 drawn beside E3 and E4 rather than above E3?

choices.text: Managing is a different job at about the same level of responsibility
choices.why: Right: the move is sideways, and the pay bands overlap.

choices.text: Managers are paid less
choices.why: Bands overlap; an E4 can earn more than an M1, not that every manager earns less.

choices.text: To save space
choices.why: The placement is the point of the figure.

choices.text: Because only E3 engineers may become managers
choices.why: Nothing restricts it that way; that is where people usually start when they cross.

prompt: At Caju, what is true of an engineer who stays at E3 for a whole career, doing excellent work?
hint: The level everybody is expected to reach.

choices.text: They are not failing
choices.why: Right: levels above E3 are optional, and require scope not everybody wants.

choices.text: They should be moved onto an improvement plan
choices.why: Nothing about staying at E3 is a performance problem.

choices.text: They will be asked to manage
choices.why: Management is a different job, not a destination for experienced engineers.

choices.text: They have reached the top of the ladder and can no longer be given any new responsibilities or scope
choices.why: E4 and E5 exist; staying at E3 is a choice, and growth without promotion is lesson 13.

prompt: At a company you are considering, nobody can reach the highest pay band without managing people. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: Nothing: pay is separate from levels
choices.why: Pay is exactly where the claim becomes real or stays a slogan.

choices.text: That it has a well-designed dual track, since managers carry the most responsibility in any company
choices.why: The lesson argues staff and principal carry comparable scope through influence.

choices.text: That it pays managers too much
choices.why: The point is about the shape of the ladder, not the size of manager pay.

choices.text: Its ladder makes management a promotion, whatever it says
choices.why: Right: if the top is only reachable by managing, people will manage to get there.
